# Part 0: Preparing Your Local LLM Workshop {#sec-chapter-00 .unnumbered}

::: {.chapter-status}
**Estimated time:** 30–45 min &nbsp;·&nbsp; **Difficulty:** 🟢 Beginner &nbsp;·&nbsp; No prior programming experience assumed
:::

## Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

- Install Python and confirm it works
- Get a copy of this book's companion repository onto your own machine
- Create and activate a virtual environment for this book
- Install this book's dependencies
- Check whether your machine has a GPU fine-tuning can use, and know
  what to expect if it doesn't
- Run `setup_check.py` and get a clean bill of health before Chapter 1

## 0.1 Why this chapter exists

Every chapter from here on assumes four things are already true: Python
is installed, this repository is on your machine, a virtual environment
for it is active, and this book's packages are installed inside that
environment. None of that is difficult, but skipping or rushing it is
the single most common reason a reader gets stuck before Chapter 1 even
starts — usually with a confusing error that has nothing to do with
drilling, completions, or language models, and everything to do with one
of these four things not being true yet.

This chapter does all four, one step at a time, with no assumption that
you've done any of it before.

::: {.callout-tip title="Already comfortable with Python and virtual environments?"}
Skip the explanations in **0.2** (installing Python), **0.6** (hardware
check), and **0.7** (choosing an editor) — you already know that part.
You still need to actually do **0.3** (clone this repository), **0.4**
(create this book's own virtual environment), **0.5** (install its
requirements), and **0.8** (run the setup check) like everyone else —
they're specific to this book, not to Python in general — but you can
move through them fast. If 0.8 comes back clean, you're done with this
chapter.
:::

## 0.2 Install Python

This book targets **Python 3.11 or later** — the same version pinned in
`requirements.txt` and `environment.yml`.

::: {.callout-tip title="Engineering Translation: what is Python, here?"}
Python is the programming language every script in this book is written
in. Installing it is like installing the one piece of shop equipment
every other tool in this book plugs into — nothing past this section
runs without it.
:::

**macOS:** Python 3 usually needs to be installed explicitly (the
system's built-in `python3` is often older or missing entirely).
Download the latest 3.11+ installer from
[python.org/downloads](https://www.python.org/downloads/) and run it, or
if you have [Homebrew](https://brew.sh) installed:

```bash
brew install python@3.11
```

**Windows:** download the installer from
[python.org/downloads](https://www.python.org/downloads/). On the first
installer screen, check **"Add python.exe to PATH"** before clicking
Install — this is the step almost everyone forgets, and it's what
Section 0.11 below assumes you didn't.

**Linux:** most distributions ship Python 3, but check the version — it
may be older than 3.11. On Ubuntu/Debian:

```bash
sudo apt update && sudo apt install python3 python3-venv python3-pip
```

**Confirm it worked:**

```bash
python3 --version
```

**Expected output:** something like `Python 3.11.9` (any 3.11 or later
patch version is fine). If you see `command not found` or a version
below 3.11, revisit the install step for your platform above.

## 0.3 Clone this repository

If you're comfortable with `git`:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/djimrastephane/llm-ft-drilling-completions-book.git
cd llm-ft-drilling-completions-book
```

Never used `git` before? Click the **Download ZIP** button on the
repository's GitHub page instead, unzip it, and open a terminal inside
the unzipped folder.

**Expected output:** a folder named
`llm-ft-drilling-completions-book` (or similar) containing, among other
things, a `book/` folder — everything from here on happens inside `book/`.

```bash
cd book
```

## 0.4 Create and activate a virtual environment

::: {.callout-tip title="Engineering Translation: what is a virtual environment?"}
A virtual environment is a private, self-contained set of Python
packages just for this project — like a dedicated toolbox for this book
that doesn't get mixed up with tools installed for anything else on your
machine. Without it, this book's packages (and their exact versions)
could conflict with something else Python-related already on your
system.
:::

From inside `book/`:

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
```

**What just happened?** This created a `.venv` folder holding a private
copy of Python and an empty toolbox, specific to this project.

Now activate it — you'll need to do this every time you open a new
terminal window to work on this book:

```bash
source .venv/bin/activate          # macOS/Linux
.venv\Scripts\activate             # Windows (Command Prompt or PowerShell)
```

**Expected result:** your terminal prompt now starts with `(.venv)`.
That prefix is your confirmation the virtual environment is active —
if it's missing, the next step will install packages into the wrong
place.

## 0.5 Install requirements

With `(.venv)` showing in your prompt and still inside `book/`:

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

**What just happened?** `pip` read the list of packages this book needs
— `transformers`, `torch`, `peft`, and the rest — and installed them
into your `.venv`. `torch` in particular is a large download (several
hundred MB to a few GB depending on platform and whether a GPU build is
selected), so this step can take a few minutes even on a fast
connection. That's normal.

**Expected output:** a long scroll of `Downloading...` and
`Installing collected packages...` lines, ending with something like
`Successfully installed torch-... transformers-... peft-... ...` and no
red `ERROR` lines.

::: {.callout-note title="bitsandbytes and your platform"}
`requirements.txt` installs `bitsandbytes` (used for 4-/8-bit QLoRA
fine-tuning) only on Linux — it has no working build for macOS. If
you're on macOS or a CPU-only machine, this is expected and not an
error; Chapter 5 explains the full-precision LoRA path you'll use
instead.
:::

## 0.6 Check your hardware

Fine-tuning, even the parameter-efficient kind this book uses, is more
sensitive to your hardware than simply running a model is. This section
doesn't require you to buy anything — it just sets expectations for
later chapters.

```{python}
#| eval: false
import torch

if torch.cuda.is_available():
    print(f"CUDA GPU available: {torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)}")
elif torch.backends.mps.is_available():
    print("Apple Silicon MPS device available")
else:
    print("No GPU detected -- CPU-only.")
```

**What just happened?** This checks for three possibilities: an
NVIDIA GPU (`cuda`), an Apple Silicon Mac's built-in accelerator
(`mps`), or neither.

**What this means for you:**

- **CUDA GPU:** the most comfortable path. Chapter 5's fine-tune, and
  the heavier Part II chapters, will run in minutes.
- **Apple Silicon MPS:** works well for this book's small models, though
  somewhat slower than a dedicated CUDA GPU.
- **CPU-only:** every chapter is still designed to run — you'll use a
  smaller model and fewer training steps where a chapter calls for it,
  at the cost of longer wait times, not a dead end.

## 0.7 Choose your workshop (editor or notebook)

You don't need a specific editor to follow this book. Pick whichever of
these you're most comfortable with — there is no wrong choice, and all
five run the exact same code:

| Environment | Recommended for | Guide |
|---|---|---|
| Jupyter Notebook | Learning and experimentation | [Appendix A1](../appendix/appendix_a1_jupyter.qmd) |
| VS Code | General coding | [Appendix A2](../appendix/appendix_a2_vscode.qmd) |
| PyCharm Community | Larger projects | [Appendix A3](../appendix/appendix_a3_pycharm.qmd) |
| Positron | Data science workflows | [Appendix A4](../appendix/appendix_a4_positron.qmd) |
| Terminal only | Minimal setup | [Appendix A5](../appendix/appendix_a5_terminal.qmd) |

If you're not sure, Jupyter Notebook or VS Code are the most common
starting points. You can always switch later — nothing in this book
locks you into one choice.

## 0.8 Run the setup check

With `(.venv)` active and requirements installed, from inside `book/`:

```bash
python code/setup_check.py
```

**Expected output:**

```
Fine-Tuning Local LLM for Drilling & Completions -- setup check

[OK] Python 3.11.9
[OK] torch importable
[OK] transformers importable
[OK] peft importable
[OK] datasets importable
[OK] accelerate importable
[INFO] No GPU detected -- CPU-only. Fine-tuning chapters will still work with a small model, just more slowly.

Workshop is ready.
```

(Your `[INFO]` line will instead name a CUDA GPU or MPS if you have one
— see Section 0.6.)

If you instead see any `[FAIL]` line, do not continue to Chapter 1 yet
— see Section 0.11, Troubleshooting, below.

## 0.9 Optional: install a local model runtime

Chapters 1–13 use `transformers` and `peft` directly — nothing here
requires any additional software. If you'd also like a familiar,
general-purpose way to run local models outside this book's own code
(useful later for quick comparisons), [Ollama](https://ollama.com) is a
convenient optional install:

```bash
# after installing from ollama.com
ollama pull qwen2.5:7b-instruct
ollama serve
```

This step is entirely optional and can be skipped for now.

## 0.10 First success checkpoint

You are ready for Chapter 1 when:

::: {.callout-caution title="CHECKPOINT — Part 0"}
- [x] `python3 --version` reports 3.11 or later
- [x] This repository is on your machine, with a `book/` folder
- [x] Your terminal prompt shows `(.venv)`
- [x] `pip install -r requirements.txt` finished with no `ERROR` lines
- [x] `python code/setup_check.py` printed `Workshop is ready.`
:::

If every box above is true, you're done with Part 0.

## 0.11 Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| `command not found: python3` (Windows) | Python wasn't added to `PATH` during install — re-run the installer and check "Add python.exe to PATH" (Section 0.2). |
| `python3 --version` shows a version below 3.11 | You have an older Python 3 install alongside a newer one; try `python3.11 --version` explicitly, or reinstall from python.org. |
| Prompt never shows `(.venv)` after activating | Confirm you ran the activate command from *inside* `book/`, and that `.venv/` actually exists there (Section 0.4). |
| `pip install -r requirements.txt` fails partway through | Re-run the same command — a partial download is the most common cause and simply retrying often finishes the job. If it fails on `torch` specifically, try `pip install torch` alone first, then re-run `pip install -r requirements.txt`. |
| `setup_check.py` reports `[FAIL] <package> not importable` | `(.venv)` isn't active, or `pip install -r requirements.txt` didn't finish successfully — re-check Sections 0.4 and 0.5. |
| `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'torch.backends'` when checking hardware | Your `torch` install didn't complete — re-run `pip install -r requirements.txt` and check for `ERROR` lines. |

## What can you do now that you couldn't do before?

You have a working Python environment, this book's dependencies
installed, and a hardware check that tells you what to expect from
later fine-tuning chapters — everything Chapter 1 assumes is already in
place.
